slides.title: Every key lives through three windows.
slides.text: A key is {hot} for 30 days: ready on every reader's device, and each new key opens the one before. Keys also turn regularly, so they {heal}: a stolen key soon opens nothing new. Then a key goes {cold}: out of the chain, so today's key no longer opens it, and into the owner's {archive}, a sealed store of old keys, opened only by the owner's own signing rules. On request, keys are {erased} everywhere.
slides.deep: Hot: back-links within the window, keys turn regularly (post-compromise security). Cold: at each rotation boundary older than the window, the chain is cut; old keys are sealed for the owner identity's archive key, split among its members by its signing rules. Late writers from before a cut lose and get a conflict view.

slides.title: Snapshots let the past go.
slides.text: At key turns older than 30 days, the history is cut: newcomers get a snapshot of the state, not the old CRDT ops, so they never see what was deleted. The older keys go to the owner's archive. A writer who comes back from before the cut loses, and sees what was not adopted.
slides.deep: Loro's shallow snapshot holds the state plus the history after a cut. Cuts happen at key-rotation boundaries older than the hot window; the old chunks' keys go to the owner's archive or are shredded on erase.

slides.title: Erasing works on any text.
slides.text: A note names ten people, and one of them asks to be forgotten. You delete their name. Then the note is {cut}: a fresh {snapshot}, the current state with no history, without the name, under a new key. The keys of everything before the cut are {shredded} on every honest device and in the archive. The name is gone for good, even from the history.
slides.deep: In the live state, a deleted character is only an ID; its content survives only in old CRDT ops, inside sealed chunks. Destroying those chunks' keys makes them unreadable everywhere (crypto-shredding). Cost: the history before the cut is gone, not just the name. Legal retention, if set, comes first.

slides.title: Some things must be kept for years.
slides.text: Bookkeeping must be kept for ten years. At any time, the owner can say {retain}: keep this until 2036. From then on, nobody can cut, shred or erase it before that date, and the date can only move later. Identities in a retention role, like your tax adviser, help keep it.
slides.deep: Retain is an owner-signed event, extend-only; honest devices refuse cuts and erasures before the date (erring toward keeping). The retention role holds want and keep, and optionally a share of the archive key. Stored as canonical CBOR; exported as JSON and PDF/A; resealed periodically under current algorithms.

slides.title: What no cryptography can do, and why that's fine.
slides.text: Whatever someone once saw, they can remember, screenshot or copy. That's true of every app today, and no system can change it. What we can promise is the rest.
list: Nothing new: rotation keeps the future out.
Nothing kept, on honest devices: the next step.
Read is per piece of data, so what you share alone is its own data.
slides.deep: The analogue hole is real for every system: whatever a reader saw can be copied. Read granularity equals key granularity, so a part shared on its own must be its own data.

slides.title: Time, in short.
list: Keys are hot for 30 days, then cold in the owner's archive.
History is cut at old key turns; newcomers get snapshots.
Erasing works on any text: delete, cut, shred.
Retain keeps things for years; nothing can undo what someone saw.
slides.deep: Heal, archive, erase and retain are one key lifecycle per piece of data.
